div.p: Software synthesis is an increasingly important problem in the design of digital signal processing systems, since multimedia systems in particular are increasingly implemented using a combination of programmable and hardwired processing elements. This paper describes new algorithms for system-level software synthesis, namely the scheduling and allocation of a set of tasks executing on a heterogeneous multiprocessor. The algorithm is hierarchical: it takes advantage of the hierarchical structure of the system's task graph to hierarchically allocate and schedule processes on the multiprocessor to meet the hard real-time constraints on the tasks. Our algorithm takes into account of both the on-chip and off-chip data communications and the behaviors of data cache memories. It can significantly improve task schedulability by carefully scheduling processes and data transfers to minimize data cache misses and off-chip data accesses.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: This paper describes new algorithms for software synthesis of multi-rate task sets on heterogeneous multiprocessors. This problem is especially important in the design of modern signal processing systems: many signal processing systems use programmable processors to implement part of their functions and the scheduling and allocation of processes is especially challenging in such heterogeneous multiprocessors. This paper focuses on one aspect of embedded system design of particular relevance to multimedia applications: memory performance. Multimedia systems rely on high-performance memory due to the large amounts of streaming data processed by the system. Performance of the instruction memory is of equal importance given the real-time requirements of multimedia computing-without proper access to instructions, critical operations may be delayed past deadlines.

Caches can be used to significantly speed up instruction access, but caches also introduce significant performance variations between best-case and worst-case behavior. Cache behavior is particularly difficult to predict when the application includes several distinct processes; multimedia systems not only contain multiple processes, but also processes that run at different rates, further complicating performance analysis. The conservative approach of assuming worst-case behavior totally ignores the cache and greatly increases the computing capability required to complete the application on time. We have developed techniques [4] which allow us to accurately estimate the effects of cache interactions between processes. The speed of this analysis lets us use these techniques to explore the design space.

The streaming nature of multimedia data makes data caches less important, but we need to take into account the performance implications of data streams on the processing architecture. This paper introduces new techniques for analyzing streaming data during the scheduling and allocation of processes on a heterogeneous multiprocessor.

To be more precise, our algorithm accepts as input set of tasks composed of multiple processes with data dependencies between them, deadlines for the tasks, and the topology of the heterogeneous multiprocessor on which the tasks are to execute. The algorithm allocates processes to processing elements and data transfers to communication links, as well as scheduling those processes and data transfers. The resulting schedule and allocation provides a software architecture for the processes which implement the operations of the tasks. Our algorithm takes advantage of the hierarchical structure of task graphs to create a high-quality software architecture in much less CPU time than previous methods. We previously developed an algorithm [SI for multi-rate task scheduling and allocation; we also introduced the first task-level model for memory hierarchies [4]; this model accurately bounds the performance of preemptive real-time tasks in presence of instruction caches and used the model to significantly improve schedulability of multi-rate tasks on multiprocessors. This paper describes new methods for handling the data transfers which are so important to multimedia and signal processing applications. Section 2 reviews previous related work. Section 3 introduces the problem formulation. Section 4 describes our allocation and scheduling algorithm in detail. Section 5 describes the results of experiments we conducted to evaluate the performance of our algorithm.

div.head: Previous Work
div.p: Related work includes studies from real-time scheduling, embedded system design and performance evaluation with cache memory.

Several groups ([ 11], [1]) have developed scheduling and allocation algorithms for a non-preemptive execution environment. These algorithms usually target a multiprocessor architecture and can handle complex tasks with precedence constraints and data communications. The metrics for these algorithms are to minimize the schedule length. However, they don't support the multi-rate systems.

Research in real-time scheduling provides an important foundation to our algorithm. In a uniprocessor environment, real-time systems commonly use one of two scheduling policies: earliest-deadline-Jirst and rate-monotonic scheduling [7]. For real-time distributed systems, especially when the tasks are multi-rate tasks with dependency constraints, the scheduling algorithms become much more complicated. Peng and Shin [8] developed a branch-and-bound algorithm for allocation of task graphs onto heterogeneous architecture. Lawler and Martel [3] showed that for a schedule of multiple periodic tasks to be feasible, each task should be scheduled repeatedly until the least-common multiple (LCM) of the periods of all tasks. Ramamritham [9] developed a heuristic scheduling algorithm which took into account data dependencies, communication, and fault-tolerance requirements. The algorithm unrolls the tasks to the LCM of the periods of the tasks. However, unrolling drastically increase the size of task graphs and creates very long schedules; it also eliminates a great deal of information about the structure of the task graph. Yen and Wolf [13] developed a co-synthesis algorithm based on rate-monotonic scheduling which can schedule complex real-time periodic tasks along with data communications, without unrolling the schedule. Li and Wolf [5] developed a hierarchical algorithm to efficiently schedule multi-rate tasks with data communications. The algorithm performs a partial unrolling which maintains still the task structure to guide scheduling.

div.head: Off-chip memories
div.p: However, most of the real-time scheduling algorithms ignore the impact of memory hierarchy can have on real-time tasks schedulability. Caches are used to improve the execution time of tasks, but in priority-driven preemptive real-time environments, the improvement is not guaranteed due to the unpredictability of cachesaverage-case improvements are of no use in systems with hard deadlines. Recent research, such as work by Rawat [IO] and also by Li, et.al [6], has developed models for analyzing the performance of a single program. While such models provide accurate estimates of the performance of a single program, they do not take into account the effects of preemptions between multiple tasks, and they are much too expensive to be used in system-level synthesis and design exploration. Kirk and Strosnider ( [2]) developed a SMART cache design that partition the cache to provide predictable cache performance. But their algorithm requires to modify the cache design in hardware. In our previous work [4], we introduced the first task-level memory model and a system-level synthesis algorithm that can take advantage of the caches when scheduling real-time multi-rate tasks. The algorithm targets at making cache behaviors predictable to some extent so that the performance improvement provided by cache can be utilized. It uses cache partitionheservation to guarantee cache hits for some tasks and therefore achieve tighter WCET bounds for these tasks. The work in 121 and [4] only modeled instruction caches. Because of the importance of data streams for multimedia and signal processing applications, in this paper, we will study how to integrate data streams especially the behaviors of data caches into task scheduling.

div.head: Problem Specification
div.p: The problem specification includes three components: a set of multi-rate realtime tasks, an architecture graph, and a technology description.

An architecture graph, shown in Figure 1 , consists of processing elements (PES), communication links, and memory elements (caches and main memory). The architecture is a multiprocessor system with multiple PES on a single chip. Each PE is As shown in Figure 2, the tasks is a set of periodic tasks, with each task represented by a DAG. Nodes represent processes, which are single execution threads, and directed edges represent data dependencies between processes. A special kind of process is data-process, represented by boxes. They are zero-execution-time dummy nodes that represents data inputs. For each out-edge of a data-process, a flag is used to indicate whether the data will be spoiled during the process execution. This is especially helpful in multimedia computing, which involves large amount of data transfer, to avoid repeated off-chip access of the same data. Each task also has a start and an end dummy node, which identifies the initiation and finishing point for the task. We assume that a process is not enabled to execute until it receives all its data. Each task is executed periodically at its specified rate. The hierarchy between the tasks and the processes is the basis of the hierarchical algorithm.

The technology description consists of two maps: the PE technology description, specifies how fast each process runs on each type of PE (not all processes need to be executable on all PE types, in which case, an infinity is used as the execution time entry); the link technology description specifies the communication time for a unit datum on each type of communication link. These times are conflict-free -they do not take into account resource preemption.

div.head: Hierarchical allocation and scheduling algorithm 4.1 Algorithm Overview caches:
div.p: We make the following assumptions about the communication links and data 0 The delay for data transfer on a type of link is proportional to the size of the data, and the inverse of the speed of the type of link. 0 The size of a local data cache is large enough for all the inpufs of a single process so that the unpreempted execution of a process does not have data cache misses once all the inputs are received.

0 A data process can generate input to several processes since the same piece of data may be needed by different processes. The data in a data process originally resides on off-chip memory (main memory). If the flag of one output of a data process indicates the data will not be destroyed, then for other outputs of the same data process, it is possible to transfer the data from on-chip.

0 If two communicating processes are allocated onto the same PE, the communication delay between the two processes is zero if data to be transferred between the two processes is never flushed out of the local data cache. Based on these assumptions, the algorithm tries to minimize data transfers especially to minimize off-chip data accesses by carefully allocating and scheduling the processes. In order to minimize data transfers, it is important for the algorithm to: allocate communication processes on same PE if appropriate; reduce preemptions which may cause data cache flushing; avoid cache overflow; and if possible, avoid repeated transfer of the data from off-chip memory.

Our algorithm uses the three-phase hierarchical approach as first introduced in our previous work [5]. The hierarchical nature of the algorithm makes it possible to construct good-quality schedules without fully unrolling all the task graphs to the LCM of their periods. As shown in Figure 3, the algorithm hierarchically constructs a schedule for the system by first computing two different schedules. First, it constructs a schedule for the processes in each task graph, assuming that the tasks executes in isolation. Next, it computes a task-level schedule for the tasks using an earliest-deadline-first policy, without looking into the task graph, except for using results of step 1 as an estimation for execution time of the tasks. Finally it creates the final system schedule by combining these two types of schedules-the results of the process schedules are combined and modified, based on the task-level schedule, to schedule each instance of every process on the multiprocessor. The details of each phase will be discussed in the following sections.

div.head: Process Scheduling Phase
div.p: The process scheduling phase is designed to create an initial local scheduling for the processes in a single task graph for one period. Each task graph is scheduled independently in this step. The cost function of the process scheduler is the minimum completion time of a task. Based on the topological relationship of processes in the task graph, the PE architecture and PE speed for different processes, and the data communications needed by the processes, the scheduler tries to find the optimal allocation and schedule for the processes and data communications.

Our algorithm schedules around critical paths in the task graph while exploring the parallelism of the processes. It is similar to that designed by Sih and Lee ill]. Figure 4 shows the outline of process scheduling phase. Initially, a static urgency is calculated for each process based upon the maximum distance of the process to the task's end. This is very similar to the priority function that is used in some list schedulers. Static urgency helps to identify the possible critical paths in the task graph. A process is scheduled by selecting a node to be scheduled next and where it will execute on at each scheduling step, based upon a dynamic urgency (see Figure 4). Dynamic urgency is based upon three terms: the static urgency of the node, the communication link congestion (based upon the input data arrival from the outputs of the processes including data processes it depends on), the availability of the PE, and the execution speed of the node on the PE. Dynamic urgency allows synthesis to simultaneously take into account allocation, scheduling, and data communications.

The scheduler saves the locations (main memory, on-chip cache in a PE, etc.) of all live data (data to be needed by processes) and updates them after every scheduling step. While calculating dynamic urgency, the communication congestion factor for a process pi on a PE PE,, is based upon the earliest data arrival time for p; on

div.head: PE,.
div.p: The scheduler checks the locations of all pi's input data, and schedules the communication links to transfer these data to PE,. If pi has a data process as one of it predecessors, then the scheduler checks if there is a unspoiled copy of this data on-chip somewhere. If the answer is yes, the data is transferred from on-chip to avoid off-chip access. Unlike list schedulers, dynamic urgency is recalculated after every scheduling selection to reflect changes in the system utilization. To save computation time, instead of calculating dynamic urgencies for all ready nodes on all possible PES at each scheduling step, the choice of ready nodes can be limited to those with high static urgencies and high volume of data and the choice of PES can be limited by user specification.

div.head: Task-level Scheduling Phase
div.p: This phase separately computes dynamic priorities for the tasks using an earliestdeadline-first (EDF) policy to preemptively schedule the PES. A priority is computed for each task (all processes in the task have the same priority since they run at the same rate). However, the EDF policy is dynamic-the algorithm computes the priority of each process running on every PE as a function of time. Figure 5 illustrates the results of this phase. We use EDF as the main scheduling policy because it creates a schedule with fewer preemptions than does rate-monotonic scheduling, under the assumption that we have some knowledge about the arrival time of processes. If two processes have identical deadlines, then a rate-monotonic policy is used to break the tie.

div.head: System Scheduling Phase
div.p: The complete system schedule is constructed from the results of the process and task-level scheduling phases. As shown in Figure 6, this phase moves through the task-level schedule in time order. The system schedule is unrolled to the leastcommon multiple of the periods. Since each process is only touched once, this scheduling phase is linear in the size of the unrolled system schedule. During unrolling, the task-level schedule is expanded so that each execution of a process is represented by the processes and data dependencies of that process. As a process instance is expanded, the process-level schedule for the process is improved based on the current state of the system schedule. A higher-priority process will be moved earlier in time if possible. This may require reallocating that process to a different PE than was originally assigned it during the process-level scheduling phase; it may also require moving a lower-priority process backward in time. Due to this repacking of the process schedules, different iterations of a process may have differ- ent schedules and allocations, measured relative to the start of the process's period.
At the end of this procedure, the complete system schedule has been constructed.

To test the effectiveness of the algorithm, we have run a number of experiments particularly multi-media applications and obtained promising results. Figure 7 shows an example with two tasks. . We schedule the tasks onto two PES. The scheduling result shown in Figure 8 eliminates most of the data transfers by allocating communicating processes to the same PE. Repeated transfer of off-chip data is avoided. In fact, the schedule in this case is optimal as verified by exhaustive search.

One of the multimedia examples that we used is the MPEG video and audio encoding algorithms [ 141. MPEG encoding involves both intensive computation and large data transfers. Scheduling the encoding algorithms to meet the real-time requirements is challenging. In the video encoder, frames are divided into blocks and the encoding is done for each block. In real time, frames arrive at the rate of 30 frames per second. In our experiment, we assume the frame resolution is' 720x480, and the block size is 16x 16, which gives 1350 blocks per frame. For the audio encoding, we use the sampling rate of 48 kHz and 16 bitdsample. We assume that the sample data are divided into sections of 1024 samples. Therefore, the rate for audio decoding is 48,000/1024 = 46.875 periods/second. The quantitative characteristics used in our experiment are summarized in Table 1.

div.p: Table 2 shows the scheduling result of the MPEG encoding algorithm on 4 identical PES of 150 MHz connected by a bus, based on the characteristics in Table 1. Our algorithm successfully schedules both audio and video encoding in real time on 4 PES while preemptions are avoided.

To show the importance of managing data streams, we compare the result of our algorithm to that of our previous algorithm [5] which tried to minimize data transfers between PES but did not optimize off-chip data transfers. This experiment used the minimum number of PES needed to meet all the real-time deadlines as the comparing measure. We use three different ratios for on-chip and off-chip data transfer speed. The results are shown in Table 3; they show that our algorithm shows increases in schedulability with increases in data transfer speed.
